content.content:
######## enforce-with-hooks
Short answer: the lines in CLAUDE.md can't make Claude do these every time. CLAUDE.md is context, and Claude usually follows it but nothing guarantees it, however firmly it is worded ("Always", "Never"). The only thing that runs every time is a hook, which Claude Code itself executes. So I'd move the five rules in your "Workflow" section into hooks in .claude/settings.json.

I ran the analyser on this project (score 93/100). It flagged four of these lines as hook candidates (lines 12, 13, 14 and 16). Line 15, the "never edit tidepool/_generated/" rule, wasn't flagged, but it is also a must-hold rule and suits a hook best of all.

Proposed mapping (nothing has been changed yet):

1. Line 12, "Always run `ruff check` after each edit": a PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write that runs `ruff check` on the file just changed. Lint errors go back to Claude straight away.
2. Line 13, "Always run `ruff format` before finishing a task": a Stop hook that runs `ruff format`. (A PostToolUse hook that formats after each edit would also work and is simpler. Which do you prefer?)
3. Line 14, "Never commit without running `pytest` first": a PreToolUse hook on Bash that spots `git commit` and runs `uv run pytest`. If the tests fail, it blocks the commit (exit code 2), so Claude sees why.
4. Line 15, "Never edit files under `tidepool/_generated/`": a PreToolUse hook on Edit|Write that blocks any path under that directory and says "regenerate instead". This is a hard block, not a request.
5. Line 16, "Run `mypy tidepool` before every commit": the same PreToolUse `git commit` hook as item 3, running `mypy tidepool` as well as pytest. One hook can cover both.

Once the hooks are in place, I'd remove lines 12, 13, 14 and 16, since the hooks do the job and the lines would only repeat them. The one exception is the "never edit _generated" line, where I'd keep a single short line saying why (the files are generated and should be regenerated). That tells Claude the reason up front, so it doesn't just run into the block. The "Commands" and "Design notes" sections are fine and I'd leave them alone.

Two things to check:
- Please confirm the commit and Stop behaviour you want. A failing pytest or mypy will block commits, and that is the point, but it does mean slow checks run on every commit.
- The analyser also reports that `tidepool/_generated` and `tidepool/parsers` can't be found. That's only because this folder holds just CLAUDE.md, so it's probably fine in your real repo. Do check the paths are spelled correctly, because the _generated hook depends on that path matching.

If you approve, I'll draft the .claude/settings.json hooks (I'd back up any existing settings first), edit CLAUDE.md as above, re-run the analyser, and then ask you to run /context and /hooks in a fresh session to confirm the hooks are registered. I won't change any file until you say yes.
######## audit-derivable-tree
I ran the analyser on this project. Your CLAUDE.md is one file of 60 lines (about 422 tokens), loaded at session start. That is well under Anthropic's 200-line recommendation, so size is not the problem. The analyser scored it 90/100. That score is the tool's own measure, not an Anthropic metric, so I'm not chasing it. I read the whole file as well, and I'd cut three sections and keep the rest.

Proposed changes, each against a named section. I haven't changed anything, and I'll only edit if you approve.

1. Delete "Project structure" (lines 5-26). This is the 18-line directory tree. Claude can list the directory itself, and the tree is already drifting: `models.py` and `base.html` are not in the project directory, so the tree has gone stale. Anthropic's best-practices page lists this kind of content as something to leave out. I'd delete it outright rather than shrink it or move it to another file.

2. Delete "Dependencies" (lines 28-37). Versions of flask, flask-sqlalchemy, pytest, ruff and the rest are in `pyproject.toml`, and Claude can read them there. A copy in CLAUDE.md can only go out of date. This is also a docs-backed finding.

3. Delete "Architecture" (lines 39-48). It is a prose overview of the app factory, the two blueprints, the models module, templates and the database. Claude can work all of that out from `app/__init__.py` and the code around it. The analyser only flagged it as a long paragraph and two stale file references, so it missed that the whole section is derivable. Rewriting it as bullets would be the wrong fix, because a section that goes needs no rewording. One line in it might be worth keeping, if it is a decision the code can't show: SQLite in development and Postgres in production. If your config already makes that obvious, drop it too. Tell me which you prefer.

Keep as they are:
- The title and one-line description.
- "Commands". These are the exact invocations for running the app, the tests and migrations. They are useful in every session.
- "Gotchas". The fractions-not-floats rule and the `SERVER_NAME` test quirk are constraints the code doesn't show.

On hooks: nothing here needs to hold every time, so I'm not proposing one. If "never store floats" must be enforced rather than advised, a hook could check for it after each edit. The CLAUDE.md line alone is only advisory.

Afterwards I'd re-run the analyser to confirm the findings are gone. Then please run `/context` in a new session and check that the Memory files list shows what you expect.

Shall I go ahead with deleting the three sections? I'll take a backup of the file first.
######## explain-context-cost
Your CLAUDE.md is about 2,800 tokens, which is small next to Claude's context window. Nothing else is adding to it. The analyser found only this one file loading for the project. The repo's own `AGENTS.md` is not loaded, because a CLAUDE.md exists. The memory directory doesn't exist in this check.

**Why it's big**

The file is 260 lines, 60 over Anthropic's recommended 200 per file. That is the only finding backed by Anthropic's docs. It loads in full at session start, so every section costs context whether or not the task touches it. I'd worry more about adherence than token count: long files tend to get followed less reliably.

About 23 sections cover quite different areas: Bookings, Pricing, API, Database, Payments, Admin, Manifests, Logging, Reports and so on. Most sessions need only a few of them.

The score is 92/100. That score is this tool's own measure, not an Anthropic metric, so I wouldn't chase it.

**What I'd suggest, if you approve**

All of this is advice. Nothing is changed, and I'd propose each edit against the named section and wait for your say-so.

1. Content for one area of the code could move to a `.claude/rules/*.md` file with `paths:` frontmatter, so it loads only when Claude touches matching files. Candidates are:
   - API (lines 68-79)
   - Database (81-92)
   - Testing (94-105)
   - Frontend (133-144)
   - Payments (181-190)
   - Staff admin (192-201)
   - Background tasks (214-223)
   - Logging (225-234)
   - Reports (236-245)
   - Manifests (203-212)

   These are the biggest wins. I'd move the text verbatim, with no rewording. I can't tell which paths each one should map to, because the fixture holds only the CLAUDE.md. Those paths are yours to give.
2. Occasional task knowledge suits a skill. Release process (156-159), Local setup (247-256) and possibly Deployment (120-131) are only needed when you're doing that task.
3. Rules that must hold every time would be better as hooks. `uv run ruff check --fix .` and `makemigrations --check` could run in a `PostToolUse` hook. Lines in CLAUDE.md are advisory only.
4. Content Claude can derive from the code can go outright. The Overview (3-7) reads like an architecture summary, and parts of Local setup (such as "copy `.env.example`") are visible from the repo. Lines that record decisions the code can't show should stay. Examples are "Booking references are never reused" and "Prices are in pence".
5. The `Contacts`, `Glossary` and `Support` sections are short and cheap. Keep them unless you want a leaner file.

Please don't split the file into `@imports` or sub-documents to shrink it. Imports load at launch together with the file that imports them, so that only reorganises the same tokens.

**Heuristic findings (my tool's judgement, so decline freely)**

- **No trigger conditions:** the tool suggests "Read X when modifying Y" lines. The `paths:` rules in point 1 do this job better.
- **Stale references:** it flagged 15 paths as not found, such as `api/`, `tests/factories.py` and `settings/production.py`. This directory holds only CLAUDE.md, so these are probably false alarms. Run the analyser against your real project root before deleting anything.

After any changes, re-run the analyser. Then run `/context` in a fresh session and check that the Memory files list shows what you expect.
######## audit-clean-file
I ran the analyser on this project, and I read the CLAUDE.md myself. It's in good shape, so I'd leave it as it is.

- Size: 22 lines, about 176 tokens, loaded at session start. That's well under Anthropic's recommended 200 lines per file.
- Findings: none, either backed by Anthropic's docs or from this tool's own judgement. The score is 100/100. That number is only this tool's own measure, so it isn't a reason to change anything.
- Content: every section earns its place.
  - The Commands section gives the test commands and says the integration tests need Docker.
  - The Gotchas section records things the code can't show on its own. These are UTC storage for timestamps, the single-threaded scheduler that is deliberate, and the shared Postgres container that needs a per-test schema.
  - The Conventions section holds two short rules.
  - There are no directory trees, dependency lists or architecture overviews to delete.
- Where things could go instead: nothing here applies to only some paths, which would call for a `paths:` rule. Nothing is occasional task knowledge, which would belong in a skill.

######## split-with-imports
Rod, splitting this into more imports won't save any context. I'd use `paths:` rules for the parts that only matter in some places, and trim the rest.

  - -3 per cross-file duplicate
  - a penalty for session cost

  - A quoted value (`description: "Use when…"`) or a folded block (`description: >`) would fail `startswith("Use when")` even though it is valid. The failure is loud, not silent, so it is a false failure, not a missed regression.
  - `test_rules_reference_has_contents_list` tests the rules reference, not the skill frontmatter, so it sits oddly in this file. That is cosmetic.

  - **"Changed" list** (`CHANGELOG.md:11-24`):

  - **"Removed" list:** upstream's README had "8-priority" (line 169) and "degrades linearly" (line 59), and neither remains.
  - **Python and dev commands:** "Python 3.13 or later" matches `pyproject.toml` `requires-python = ">=3.13"`. The README dev commands match AGENTS.md.
  - **README usage section:** `/context`, "reads the always-on files itself" and "verbatim" all match SKILL.md (steps at :49-56, verbatim rule at :93).
  - **LICENSE:** the change adds one line.
  
  ### Not judged
  - Whether "Claude Code warns that a memory file is large" (in the description) matches current Claude Code behaviour.
  - Whether the code actually needs 3.13, as opposed to 3.11 or later. I only checked that it agrees with `pyproject.toml`.

  conflicts.
- The `LICENSE` file names the fork's maintainer alongside the original
  author.

### Removed

- The "8-priority" workflow and the claim that instruction following
  "degrades linearly".

# claude-md-optimizer

A Claude Code skill that audits the instruction files Claude Code loads
(`CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/rules/`, `@` imports and
`MEMORY.md`) and helps you move each piece of content to where it works best.

This fork of [geuneda/claude-md-optimizer][upstream] is reworked to follow
Anthropic's current [memory][memory] and [best practices][anthropic] docs.

## What it does

- Finds every file Claude Code would load for a project, with its load mode:
  always, conditional (`paths:` rules), on demand, dormant, excluded or
  skipped.
- Runs checks and tags each finding by where it comes from. A `docs` finding
  cites an Anthropic page. A `heuristic` finding is this tool's own judgement
  and is offered as a suggestion.
- Lists the limits it could not confirm in Anthropic's docs as unverified,
  rather than stating them as fact.
- Scores the result from 0 to 100. The score starts at 100 and only goes

Phase 3 is done and committed locally on `chore/docs-and-description`, but not pushed and no PR is open. I need your go-ahead for both. The full suite passes (475 tests), and ruff and markdownlint are clean.

I did it inline from Task 3.1 of the plan, with one fresh Opus review of the whole branch at the end. I used `entire brain brief` and `recall` to get oriented, and the plan itself came from the planning worktree.

**What changed** (two commits: `184cead` and `4c40df7`)
- **SKILL.md description:** it now starts "Use when" and gives triggers only. It is 293 characters, with no workflow summary and no line limits.
- **`tests/test_skill_frontmatter.py`:** five new tests. Three failed before the edit. The no-line-limits test and the contents-list test passed straight away, because the rules reference already had its contents list.
- **README:** rewritten at about 100 lines. The old comparison table is gone, along with "22/100", the 8-priority order and "degrades linearly". The example report comes from the current analyser, run on the `derivable-tree` fixture.
- **CHANGELOG:** new, with the "scores are not comparable with earlier versions" note.
- **LICENSE:** a second copyright line for you.

**Scenario re-run:** all 5 scenarios pass, one rep each. The plan said four, but `tests/scenarios/` has five. Results and raw advice are committed locally on the planning branch (`669807f`) and not pushed. The runs were given the path to `SKILL.md`, so they don't test whether Claude Code actually picks the skill from the new description. That needs the skill installed and a fresh session.

**Review fixes:** the reviewer found two Important issues and I fixed both.
- The README example silently dropped findings, so its numbers didn't add up. It is now labelled as an excerpt, with `...` marking what's omitted.
- The CHANGELOG said the old score wasn't deduction-based. Upstream's score also started at 100 and deducted, so I corrected the contrast.
- I upgraded the install commands from Minor to Important, because they fail on a machine with no `~/.claude/skills`. They now use `mkdir -p`, and I checked them in a scratch directory.

**Deferred minors** (none fixed):
- README says "every other threshold is a heuristic", but the 4 MiB file limit and four-hop import depth are documented limits.
- The tests are narrow. They only ban the words "scores", "detects" and "0-100" and the numbers "150" and "50 lines". The frontmatter parsing is a single-line regex, and the contents-list test sits oddly in this file.
- The reviewer didn't judge whether "Claude Code warns that a memory file is large" matches current Claude Code behaviour, or whether the HumanLayer/Arize/Dometrain credit links still work.

**Rulings I made:**
- I used a plain branch in the main checkout, not a worktree. If wrong, the cost is one `git switch`.

# claude-md-optimizer

A Claude Code skill that audits the instruction files Claude Code loads
(`CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/rules/`, `@` imports and
`MEMORY.md`) and helps you move each piece of content to where it works best.

This fork of [geuneda/claude-md-optimizer][upstream] is reworked to follow
Anthropic's current [memory][memory] and [best practices][anthropic] docs.

## What it does

- Finds every file Claude Code would load for a project, with its load mode:
  always, conditional (`paths:` rules), on demand, dormant, excluded or
  skipped.
- Runs checks and tags each finding by where it comes from. A `docs` finding
  cites an Anthropic page. A `heuristic` finding is this tool's own judgement
  and is offered as a suggestion.
- Lists the limits it could not confirm in Anthropic's docs as unverified,
  rather than stating them as fact.
- Scores the result from 0 to 100. The score starts at 100 and only goes
  down. It is this tool's own measure, not an Anthropic metric.
- Proposes changes against named lines, applies only what you approve, and
  moves content verbatim.

## Installation

Clone the repo, then copy the skill directory into your skills directory:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer.git
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R claude-md-optimizer/claude-md-optimizer ~/.claude/skills/
```

The skill directory is `claude-md-optimizer/`. It needs Python 3.13 or later
and has no runtime dependencies.

## Usage

In Claude Code, say something like:

```text
Optimize my CLAUDE.md
```

The skill runs the analyser, reads the always-on files itself, and proposes
changes one at a time. It ends by asking you to run `/context` in a new
session to check the Memory files list.

You can also run the analyser directly. Add `--json` for machine-readable
output:

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/claude-md-optimizer/scripts/analyze_claude_md.py \
  /path/to/project
```

## Example output

An excerpt: paths are shortened, long lines wrapped, and `...` marks
omitted findings, `Fix:` lines and deductions. The score is the real total.

```text
============================================================
  CLAUDE.md Optimization Report
============================================================

  Context load (estimated tokens):
    Always-on:   ~422
    Conditional: ~0
    On demand:   ~0

    always  project  60 lines  ~422 tokens  /project/CLAUDE.md

  Unverified limits: COMBINED_LINES

------------------------------------------------------------
  Backed by Anthropic docs (2):
    [issue] derivable-content: /project/CLAUDE.md:7 looks like a
        directory tree. Claude can read this from the code or
        config, so it can usually be cut.
        Docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
    ...

  Heuristics (this tool's own judgement) (4):
    [suggestion] code-block-long: /project/CLAUDE.md:7 contains a
        code block of 18 lines (over 5).
    ...

------------------------------------------------------------
  Deductions:
    code-block-long: 1 finding(s), -1
    derivable-content: 2 finding(s), -4
    ...

  Score: 90/100 (starts at 100; only deductions apply)
============================================================
```

## What counts as documented

Anthropic recommends under 200 lines per `CLAUDE.md` file. `MEMORY.md`
loads its first 200 lines or 25KB. Every other threshold in the analyser is
a heuristic and is tagged that way. The full list of rules, check ids and
unverified items is in
[`references/optimization-rules.md`](claude-md-optimizer/references/optimization-rules.md).

## Development

```bash
uv sync
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
```

## Credits

Originally written by geuneda. Research sources: [Anthropic][anthropic],
[HumanLayer][humanlayer], [Arize][arize] and [Dometrain][dometrain].

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/claude-md-optimizer

# CLAUDE.md Optimizer

Audit the instruction files Claude Code loads for a project and move each
piece of content to the place where it works best. Read
`references/optimization-rules.md` when you need the source for a claim or
the meaning of a check id; it tags every rule `[docs]` or `[heuristic]`.

## How loading works

- CLAUDE.md files, `CLAUDE.local.md`, rules without `paths:`, their `@path`
  imports and MEMORY.md (first 200 lines or 25KB) load at session start.
  Never describe this as a cost that recurs on every request or grows with
  the number of turns.
- Imported files load at launch together with the file that imports them,
  so splitting a file into imports only reorganises it. A plain pointer
  such as "see docs/x.md" loads nothing by itself; Claude reads the file
  only if it decides the pointer applies.
- Content loads later only through mechanisms Claude Code runs itself: a
  rule with `paths:` frontmatter, a nested CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory, or
  a skill.
- CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration: no wording or emphasis
  guarantees Claude follows it. Only a hook runs every time.
- Anthropic recommends under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Every other
  threshold is this tool's own and lives in the script, not in advice.

## Workflow

1. Run the analyser (the `scripts/` directory sits next to this file):

   ```bash
   python3 scripts/analyze_claude_md.py <project-dir>
   ```

   Add `--json` for machine-readable output. The report lists each file
   with its load mode (always, conditional, on demand, dormant, excluded or
   skipped), estimated tokens by mode, the auto memory directory, the
   limits that are still unverified, findings grouped into docs-backed and
   heuristic, every deduction, and a score.
1. Read the findings by source. A docs finding cites an Anthropic page. A
   heuristic finding is this tool's judgement: offer it as a suggestion the
   user may decline. The score starts at 100 and only goes down. It is this
   tool's own measure, not an Anthropic metric, so never propose a change
   just to raise it.
1. Read every always-on file yourself. The checks match patterns and miss
   things, such as an architecture overview written as prose. Choose a
   destination for each section from the table below before acting on any
   finding about its form; a section you delete needs no rewording.
1. Propose each change against a named existing line or section, with its
   reason, and apply only what the user approves.
1. Re-run the analyser. Then ask the user to run `/context` in a new session
   and check that the Memory files list shows what they expect.

Claude Code's built-in `/doctor` complements this: its checkup proposes
trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md, and `/doctor prompt-audit` looks for
outdated or conflicting instructions.

## Destinations

| Content | Destination |
| --- | --- |
| Needed in every session | Stays in CLAUDE.md |
| Applies to some paths only | `paths:` rule or nested CLAUDE.md |
| Occasional task knowledge | A skill |
| Must happen every time | A hook in settings |
| Claude can derive it from code | Delete, with approval |
| Notes for human maintainers | A block-level HTML comment |
| Personal notes for this project | `CLAUDE.local.md` |

- Derivable content means directory trees, dependency lists, architecture
  overviews and file-by-file descriptions. Delete it outright. Do not keep a
  condensed version or move it to another file. A single line recording a
  decision or constraint the code cannot show may stay.
- For a rule that has to hold every time, propose a hook: for example
  `PostToolUse` to run a check once an edit lands, or `PreToolUse` to block an
  edit or a command. Tell the user the CLAUDE.md line alone is advisory.
- Do not create new imports or sub-documents to shrink context. Use the
  mechanisms in the table, which Claude Code loads for you when they apply.
  Correct any text that claims an import loads on demand.
- If the analyser finds nothing and no row above applies, say the file is in
  good shape and leave it. Do not add sections, reformat or reorder lines,
  or suggest splits for some future size. Every proposed change needs a
  functional reason.

## Safety rules

- Never modify a file without the user's explicit approval.
- Back up the original files before restructuring.
- Move content verbatim. Never summarise or paraphrase while moving it.
- After each extraction, verify zero information loss: every line is still
  present, moved verbatim, or deleted with approval.
- Keep unlock instructions inline. If an instruction is needed to reach or
  use other content (for example how to decrypt or authenticate first), it
  stays next to that content.
- Keep content that CI or scripts parse, in the form they expect.

import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
FORK = "rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer"


def run(script: str, command: str) -> int:
    payload = json.dumps({"tool_input": {"command": command}})
    return subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, str(HERE / script)], input=payload, text=True,
        capture_output=True,
    ).returncode


NO_VERIFY_BLOCK = [
    "git commit --no-verify -m x",
    "git commit -n -m x",
    "git commit -nm x",
    "git commit -anm x",
    "git push --no-verify",
    "git add . && git commit --no-verify -m 'x'",
    "git -C /tmp/r commit --no-verify -m x",
    "git merge --no-verify topic",
]
NO_VERIFY_ALLOW = [
    "git commit -m 'run next step'",
    "git commit -am 'x'",
    "git commit -m 'mention --no-verify in a message'",
    "git push -n",
    "git commit --amend --no-edit",
    "git status",
    "echo hello",
    "git commit -m 'unbalanced quote",
]
GH_BLOCK = [
    "gh pr create --title x",
    "gh pr create --repo geuneda/claude-md-optimizer",
    f"gh pr merge 7 --repo geuneda/claude-md-optimizer --merge",
    "gh issue comment 4 --body hi",
    "cd x && gh pr ready 7",
    "gh api repos/geuneda/claude-md-optimizer/issues -f title=x",
    "gh api -X POST repos/geuneda/claude-md-optimizer/issues",
    "gh release create v1",
]
GH_ALLOW = [
    f"gh pr create --repo {FORK} --draft",
    f"gh pr merge 7 --repo {FORK} --merge",
    f"gh pr create -R {FORK}",
    f"gh pr create --repo={FORK}",
    "gh pr view 7",
    "gh pr list --repo geuneda/claude-md-optimizer",
    "gh pr checks 7 || true",
    f"gh api repos/{FORK}/issues -f title=x",
    "gh api repos/geuneda/claude-md-optimizer/issues",
    "echo 'gh pr create is blocked'",
    "git status",
]


def check(script, cases, expected):
    failures = [c for c in cases if run(script, c) != expected]
    print(f"{script}: {len(cases) - len(failures)}/{len(cases)} "
          f"{'blocked' if expected == 2 else 'allowed'} as expected")
    for c in failures:
        print("   WRONG:", c)
    return not failures


ok = all([
    check("block-no-verify.py", NO_VERIFY_BLOCK, 2),
    check("block-no-verify.py", NO_VERIFY_ALLOW, 0),
    check("require-gh-repo.py", GH_BLOCK, 2),
    check("require-gh-repo.py", GH_ALLOW, 0),
])
sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)

# AGENTS.md

This file provides guidance to coding agents (including Claude Code) when
working with code in this repository.

## What this repo is

A Claude Code skill (`claude-md-optimizer/`) that audits `CLAUDE.md` files,
plus a Python analyser it runs. This is Rod's fork of geuneda's upstream; work
here is fork-only, not for upstream PRs. The skill is being reworked to match
Anthropic's current memory docs.

The skill directory is the shippable unit: `SKILL.md` is the prompt,
`references/optimization-rules.md` holds the rules, and `scripts/` holds the
analyser.

## Commands

Python 3.13+, managed with `uv`. There are no runtime dependencies.

```bash
uv sync                                  # install pytest and ruff
uv run pytest                            # full suite
uv run pytest tests/test_limits.py       # one file
uv run pytest tests/test_model.py::test_name   # one test
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
python3 claude-md-optimizer/scripts/analyze_claude_md.py <project-dir> [--json]
```

`pytest` puts `claude-md-optimizer/scripts` on `pythonpath`, so tests import
`claude_md.*` directly.

## Architecture

`scripts/analyze_claude_md.py` is a thin CLI wrapper: `discover()`, then
`run_checks()`, `score()` and `render()` (or JSON). All logic lives in the
`claude_md` package.

The `claude_md` package models what Claude Code actually loads:

- `discovery.py`: `discover()` walks managed, user, ancestor, project, local,
  rules, nested, `@import` and auto-memory files. It returns `LoadedFile`s in
  load order. It also handles `.claude/settings.json` excludes, git
  worktree-to-main-repo mapping, and `AGENTS.md` as a fallback that only loads
  when no `CLAUDE.md` exists at or above the working directory.
- `model.py`: `Scope` (where a file came from), `LoadMode` (always,
  conditional via `paths:` frontmatter, on-demand, excluded, dormant,
  skipped), `LoadedFile`, and `totals()`.
- `limits.py`: documented limits as `Limit(value, verified, source)`.
  Anything not confirmed by Anthropic's docs has `verified=False` and is
  surfaced as "unverified" in the report. Do not state a limit as fact unless
  it is verified.
- `text.py`: token estimate, HTML-comment stripping, frontmatter and `paths:`
  parsing.
- `findings.py`: the check registry. `@check(id, source, weight, cap)`
  registers a function that returns `Finding`s. `source` is `docs` (with a
  page URL) or `heuristic` (no URL).
- `checks/`: one module per group of checks. Importing `claude_md.checks`
  registers them, so a new module needs a line in `checks/__init__.py`.
  Shared helpers are in `_markdown.py` and `_common.py`; use
  `text.fence_step` for fenced-code state, never a new copy.
- `scoring.py`, `report.py`: the score starts at 100 and only goes down
  (`min(cap, weight * count)` per check id). `render()` groups findings by
  source tag.

Each check chooses its files. `checks/_common.py` `loaded()` gives always-on,
conditional and non-memory on-demand files; size and trigger checks narrow to
always-on, and `duplicate-across` to always-on and conditional.

## Writing checks

- Report lines from `file.source_text` (removed frontmatter and comment lines
  stay as blanks, so numbers match the file on disk). Use `file.text` for
  sizes, tokens and whole-text matching.
- Messages must not claim per-request or compounding cost; tests grep for
  "per request", "turns", "compound" and "session cost".
- Adding or removing a check: update the id pin in `tests/test_final_fixes.py`
  and the fixtures' `expected.json`. The `clean` fixture must stay at zero
  findings.
- `test_scoring.py` asserts heuristic caps total less than docs caps. Run it
  before changing any weight or cap.

## Tests

- `tests/test_*.py` drive the analyser through the CLI. The `tree` fixture
  builds a file tree in `tmp_path`, and `run_cli` runs the script with `HOME`
  set to `tmp_path/home`. Always pass a project subdirectory such as
  `root / "project"`, never `tmp_path` itself, or the fake home is analysed as
  project content.
- `tests/fixtures/<name>/{project/,expected.json}` are sample projects;
  `test_fixtures_wellformed.py` validates their shape. Run them from a copy
  in `tmp_path`: in place, the repo's own `AGENTS.md` is an ancestor and
  leaks into the findings.
- `tests/scenarios/` are manual, agent-run checks of the skill's advice, not
  pytest. Follow the run and isolation protocol in `tests/scenarios/README.md`
  exactly (fresh subagent, explicit skill path, `HOME` override, 3 reps).
- `test_known_bugs.py` pins fixed discovery bugs.

## Repo conventions

- Markdown must be markdownlint-clean (lines under 80 characters, blank lines
  around blocks). The Entire-managed block at the end of this file is longer
  than that and reports MD013; leave it alone.
- Phase plans, specs and baselines live only on branch
  `planning/claude-md-optimizer-rework`. Never merge them to `main`.
- Work is phased, and each phase ends in a draft PR to `main` on the fork (see
  "GitHub: fork only" below).
- `git push` runs Entire's hook. The first branch push is often rejected;
  confirm the remote did not move, retry once, and never force.
- `.claude/`, `.codex/` and `.entire/` configs are tracked and belong to the
  Entire integration. `.agent-traces/` and `.private-journal/` are not.

## GitHub: fork only

- Every GitHub interaction MUST happen on Rod's fork,
  `rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer`. That covers PRs, issues, comments, reviews,
  labels, releases and repo settings.
- NEVER open a PR or an issue, or post anything else, on the upstream repo
  (`geuneda/claude-md-optimizer`). This work is fork-only and is not for
  upstream.
- Always pass `--repo rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer` to `gh`, because `gh`
  defaults to upstream after forking. Check the target repo before any `gh`
  command that writes.
- The `upstream` remote is read-only. Never push to it. Push branches to
  `origin` and open PRs against `main` on the fork.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/plugins/cache/entire-skills/entire/0.7.4/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

HOOK = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / ".claude/hooks/require-gh-repo.py"
FORK = "rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer"
UPSTREAM = "geuneda/claude-md-optimizer"


def run_hook(command: str) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
    payload = json.dumps({"tool_input": {"command": command}})
    return subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, str(HOOK)],
        input=payload,
        text=True,
        capture_output=True,
        check=False,
    )


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "command",
    [
        "gh pr create --title x",
        f"gh pr create --repo {UPSTREAM}",
        f"gh pr merge 7 --repo {UPSTREAM} --merge",
        "gh issue comment 4 --body hi",
        "cd x && gh pr ready 7",
        f"gh api repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues -f title=x",
        f"gh api -X POST repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues",
        "gh release create v1",
        "echo $(gh pr create --title x)",
        "GH_TOKEN=x gh pr create --title t",
        "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh pr create --title t",
        "command gh pr create --title t",
        "env GH_TOKEN=x gh pr create --title t",
        "git status\ngh pr create --title t",
        "x=`gh pr create --title t`",
        'bash -c "gh pr create --title t"',
        "sh -c 'cd x && gh pr create'",
        "eval gh pr create --title t",
        "echo pr | xargs gh",
        f"gh api --method=POST repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues",
        f"gh api -XPOST repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues",
        f"gh api repos/{FORK}-evil/issues -f title=x",
        f"gh api repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues -f body=repos/{FORK}",
        "gh api graphql -f query=x",
        "gh repo fork",
        "gh repo sync",
        f"gh workflow run ci.yml --repo {UPSTREAM}",
        "gh secret set TOKEN",
        "gh run rerun 123",
        "gh variable set X",
        "gh cache delete --all",
        "gh pr create --title \"it's (unterminated quote",
        'gh issue comment 1 --body "oops',
    ],
)
def test_blocks_writes_not_aimed_at_the_fork(command):
    result = run_hook(command)
    assert result.returncode == 2
    assert "fork-only" in result.stderr


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "command",
    [
        f"gh pr create --repo {FORK} --draft",
        f"gh pr merge 7 --repo {FORK} --merge",
        f"gh pr create -R {FORK}",
        f"gh pr create --repo={FORK}",
        "gh pr view 7",
        f"gh pr list --repo {UPSTREAM}",
        "gh pr checks 7 || true",
        f"gh api repos/{FORK}/issues -f title=x",
        f"gh api repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues",
        f"gh api repos/{FORK}-x/issues",
        f"gh api --method=GET repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues -f state=open",
        f"gh api -H 'Accept: x' -X POST repos/{FORK}/issues",
        "echo 'gh pr create is blocked'",
        "git status",
        "echo unterminated 'quote",
        f"gh pr create --repo {FORK.upper()}",
        f"gh pr create --repo github.com/{FORK}",
        f"gh pr create --repo https://github.com/{FORK}.git",
        f"gh repo edit {FORK} --description x",
        "gh run list",
        "gh workflow view ci.yml",
        "gh auth status",
        "gh gist create notes.txt",
        f"GH_TOKEN=x gh pr create --repo {FORK}",
        f"bash -c 'gh pr merge 7 --repo {FORK}'",
        "git log --oneline\ngit status",
    ],
)
def test_allows_reads_and_fork_writes(command):
    assert run_hook(command).returncode == 0

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""PreToolUse hook (matcher: Bash): gh writes must target the fork."""
3	
4	import json
5	import shlex
6	import sys
7	
8	FORK = "rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer"
9	OPERATORS = {";", "&&", "||", "|", "&", "(", ")"}
10	WRITE_VERBS = {
11	    "pr": {
12	        "create",
13	        "edit",
14	        "comment",
15	        "merge",
16	        "ready",
17	        "close",
18	        "reopen",
19	        "review",
20	        "revert",
21	        "update-branch",
22	    },
23	    "issue": {
24	        "create",
25	        "edit",
26	        "comment",
27	        "close",
28	        "reopen",
29	        "delete",
30	        "transfer",
31	        "pin",
32	        "unpin",
33	        "lock",
34	        "unlock",
35	    },
36	    "release": {"create", "edit", "delete", "upload", "delete-asset"},
37	    "label": {"create", "edit", "delete", "clone"},
38	    "repo": {"edit", "delete", "rename", "archive", "unarchive"},
39	}
40	API_WRITE_METHODS = {"POST", "PATCH", "PUT", "DELETE"}
41	
42	
43	def segments(command: str) -> list[list[str]]:
44	    lexer = shlex.shlex(command, posix=True, punctuation_chars=True)
45	    lexer.whitespace_split = True
46	    result: list[list[str]] = [[]]
47	    for token in lexer:
48	        if token in OPERATORS:
49	            result.append([])
50	        else:
51	            result[-1].append(token)
52	    return [segment for segment in result if segment]
53	
54	
55	def repo_flag(args: list[str]) -> str | None:
56	    for i, arg in enumerate(args):
57	        if arg in ("--repo", "-R") and i + 1 < len(args):
58	            return args[i + 1]
59	        if arg.startswith("--repo="):
60	            return arg.split("=", 1)[1]
61	    return None
62	
63	
64	def api_is_write(args: list[str]) -> bool:
65	    for i, arg in enumerate(args):
66	        if arg in ("-X", "--method") and i + 1 < len(args):
67	            return args[i + 1].upper() in API_WRITE_METHODS
68	        if arg in ("-f", "-F", "--field", "--raw-field", "--input"):
69	            return True
70	    return False
71	
72	
73	def problem(tokens: list[str]) -> str | None:
74	    if not tokens or tokens[0] != "gh":
75	        return None
76	    args = tokens[1:]
77	    if args[:1] == ["api"]:
78	        if api_is_write(args) and f"repos/{FORK}" not in " ".join(args):
79	            return f"gh api writes must use a path under repos/{FORK}"
80	        return None
81	    if len(args) >= 2 and args[1] in WRITE_VERBS.get(args[0], set()):
82	        repo = repo_flag(args)
83	        if repo != FORK:
84	            return f"gh {args[0]} {args[1]} needs --repo {FORK} (got {repo})"
85	    return None
86	
87	
88	def main() -> int:
89	    command = json.load(sys.stdin).get("tool_input", {}).get("command", "")
90	    try:
91	        problems = [p for s in segments(command) if (p := problem(s))]
92	    except ValueError:
93	        problems = []
94	    if problems:
95	        print(
96	            "Blocked: " + "; ".join(problems) + ". This project is fork-only: "
97	            "never post to geuneda/claude-md-optimizer.",
98	            file=sys.stderr,
99	        )
100	        return 2
101	    return 0
102	
103	
104	if __name__ == "__main__":
105	    sys.exit(main())

I resolved 7 of the 9 findings on the trail and left 2 open for you. The changes are in the working tree, uncommitted and unpushed, on `chore/gh-repo-hook`. The full suite passes (534 tests) and ruff and format are clean.

No trail number was given, so I used the branch name as the selector. The 3 high findings, 3 of the 4 medium and 1 low were all about gaps in `require-gh-repo.py`. None had a suggested patch, so I fixed them by hand, with the failing tests written first (28 failed, then all 59 hook tests passed).

**Resolved**
- **High, gh api write detection:** it now parses `--method=POST` and `-XPOST`. It takes the first positional argument as the endpoint and requires `repos/<fork>` or `repos/<fork>/...`. Look-alike names such as `...-evil` and a fork name hidden in a `-f body=` field no longer pass.
- **High, newline between commands:** unquoted newlines and backticks are now command separators. Quoted heredoc bodies are unaffected.
- **High, env vars, wrappers, absolute paths:** it skips `NAME=x` prefixes and wrappers like `env`, `command`, `sudo` and `xargs`. It compares the program's basename to `gh`, and looks inside `bash -c`, `sh -c` and `eval`.
- **Medium, tests:** I added a block or allow case for every shape in the finding. That includes a GET to `repos/FORK-x/issues`, which is allowed.
- **Medium, fails open on unparseable commands:** it now falls back to a regex and fails closed unless the fork is named.
- **Medium, verb denylist:** it is now a read-only allowlist. Any other `gh <group> <verb>` needs the fork. `gh repo fork`, `gh workflow run`, `gh secret set` and similar are blocked.
- **Low, case-sensitive repo name:** matching is now case-insensitive and accepts `github.com/` and `https://` forms, with `.git` stripped.

**Left open for your decision**
1. **Medium, `AGENTS.md:120`:** the reviewer wants a short `--repo` line restored so non-Claude agents (the repo tracks `.codex/` too) still get the rule. That reverses what you told me to remove. Do you want it back?
2. **Low, `.claude/settings.json:34`:** the hook entry sits in a file Entire also writes, and a reinstall might drop it. Testing that means running an Entire setup command, which I leave to you. You chose that location knowingly. The alternatives are `settings.local.json` or a note in `AGENTS.md`.

**Things to know**
- **Rulings I made:** the groups `gist`, `ssh-key`, `gpg-key`, `codespace` and `project` are exempt, since `--repo` can't apply to account-level commands. `gh repo ...` also accepts the fork as a positional argument, because those subcommands don't take `--repo`. If either is wrong, it's an edit to the exempt list.
- **Fail-closed cost:** an unquoted heredoc that contains an apostrophe and the text `gh pr create` is now blocked, because the hook can't parse it. I found this one false positive. Quoted heredocs, which I use for PR and commit bodies, pass. I tried eight realistic commands from this session.

Commit and push this to PR #8 when you're ready.

# AGENTS.md

This file provides guidance to coding agents (including Claude Code) when
working with code in this repository.

## What this repo is

A Claude Code skill (`claude-md-optimizer/`) that audits `CLAUDE.md` files,
plus a Python analyser it runs. This is Rod's fork of geuneda's upstream; work
here is fork-only, not for upstream PRs. The skill is being reworked to match
Anthropic's current memory docs.

The skill directory is the shippable unit: `SKILL.md` is the prompt,
`references/optimization-rules.md` holds the rules, and `scripts/` holds the
analyser.

## Commands

Python 3.13+, managed with `uv`. There are no runtime dependencies.

```bash
uv sync                                  # install pytest and ruff
uv run pytest                            # full suite
uv run pytest tests/test_limits.py       # one file
uv run pytest tests/test_model.py::test_name   # one test
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
python3 claude-md-optimizer/scripts/analyze_claude_md.py <project-dir> [--json]
```

`pytest` puts `claude-md-optimizer/scripts` on `pythonpath`, so tests import
`claude_md.*` directly.

## Architecture

`scripts/analyze_claude_md.py` is a thin CLI wrapper: `discover()`, then
`run_checks()`, `score()` and `render()` (or JSON). All logic lives in the
`claude_md` package.

The `claude_md` package models what Claude Code actually loads:

- `discovery.py`: `discover()` walks managed, user, ancestor, project, local,
  rules, nested, `@import` and auto-memory files. It returns `LoadedFile`s in
  load order. It also handles `.claude/settings.json` excludes, git
  worktree-to-main-repo mapping, and `AGENTS.md` as a fallback that only loads
  when no `CLAUDE.md` exists at or above the working directory.
- `model.py`: `Scope` (where a file came from), `LoadMode` (always,
  conditional via `paths:` frontmatter, on-demand, excluded, dormant,
  skipped), `LoadedFile`, and `totals()`.
- `limits.py`: documented limits as `Limit(value, verified, source)`.
  Anything not confirmed by Anthropic's docs has `verified=False` and is
  surfaced as "unverified" in the report. Do not state a limit as fact unless
  it is verified.
- `text.py`: token estimate, HTML-comment stripping, frontmatter and `paths:`
  parsing.
- `findings.py`: the check registry. `@check(id, source, weight, cap)`
  registers a function that returns `Finding`s. `source` is `docs` (with a
  page URL) or `heuristic` (no URL).
- `checks/`: one module per group of checks. Importing `claude_md.checks`
  registers them, so a new module needs a line in `checks/__init__.py`.
  Shared helpers are in `_markdown.py` and `_common.py`; use
  `text.fence_step` for fenced-code state, never a new copy.
- `scoring.py`, `report.py`: the score starts at 100 and only goes down
  (`min(cap, weight * count)` per check id). `render()` groups findings by
  source tag.

Each check chooses its files. `checks/_common.py` `loaded()` gives always-on,
conditional and non-memory on-demand files; size and trigger checks narrow to
always-on, and `duplicate-across` to always-on and conditional.

## Writing checks

- Report lines from `file.source_text` (removed frontmatter and comment lines
  stay as blanks, so numbers match the file on disk). Use `file.text` for
  sizes, tokens and whole-text matching.
- Messages must not claim per-request or compounding cost; tests grep for
  "per request", "turns", "compound" and "session cost".
- Adding or removing a check: update the id pin in `tests/test_final_fixes.py`
  and the fixtures' `expected.json`. The `clean` fixture must stay at zero
  findings.
- `test_scoring.py` asserts heuristic caps total less than docs caps. Run it
  before changing any weight or cap.

## Tests

- `tests/test_*.py` drive the analyser through the CLI. The `tree` fixture
  builds a file tree in `tmp_path`, and `run_cli` runs the script with `HOME`
  set to `tmp_path/home`. Always pass a project subdirectory such as
  `root / "project"`, never `tmp_path` itself, or the fake home is analysed as
  project content.
- `tests/fixtures/<name>/{project/,expected.json}` are sample projects;
  `test_fixtures_wellformed.py` validates their shape. Run them from a copy
  in `tmp_path`: in place, the repo's own `AGENTS.md` is an ancestor and
  leaks into the findings.
- `tests/scenarios/` are manual, agent-run checks of the skill's advice, not
  pytest. Follow the run and isolation protocol in `tests/scenarios/README.md`
  exactly (fresh subagent, explicit skill path, `HOME` override, 3 reps).
- `test_known_bugs.py` pins fixed discovery bugs.

## Repo conventions

- Markdown must be markdownlint-clean (lines under 80 characters, blank lines
  around blocks). The Entire-managed block at the end of this file is longer
  than that and reports MD013; leave it alone.
- Phase plans, specs and baselines live only on branch
  `planning/claude-md-optimizer-rework`. Never merge them to `main`.
- Work is phased, and each phase ends in a draft PR to `main` on the fork (see
  "GitHub: fork only" below).
- `git push` runs Entire's hook. The first branch push is often rejected;
  confirm the remote did not move, retry once, and never force.
- `.claude/`, `.codex/` and `.entire/` configs are tracked and belong to the
  Entire integration. `.agent-traces/` and `.private-journal/` are not.

## GitHub: fork only

- Every GitHub interaction MUST happen on Rod's fork,
  `rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer`. That covers PRs, issues, comments, reviews,
  labels, releases and repo settings.
- NEVER open a PR or an issue, or post anything else, on the upstream repo
  (`geuneda/claude-md-optimizer`). This work is fork-only and is not for
  upstream.
- The `upstream` remote is read-only. Never push to it. Push branches to
  `origin` and open PRs against `main` on the fork.

input.content:
Drafted by Claude (an agent running under Rod's direction).

The AGENTS.md instruction "always pass `--repo` to `gh`" was only advisory.
A miss posts to upstream, so a hook that Claude Code runs every time now
enforces it.

## Changes

- `.claude/hooks/require-gh-repo.py`: a `PreToolUse` hook on Bash. A `gh`
  command is allowed if it is read-only, not repo-scoped, or names
  `rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer`. Anything else is blocked.
  - Read-only verbs: `view`, `list`, `status`, `checks`, `diff`, `checkout`,
    `download`, `watch`, `clone`, `browse`, `get`. Any other `gh <group>
    <verb>` needs the fork, so `gh repo fork`, `gh workflow run`,
    `gh secret set` and similar are blocked.
  - Groups that cannot take `--repo` (`auth`, `config`, `gist`, `ssh-key`,
    `codespace` and so on) are exempt.
  - `gh api` writes need an endpoint equal to or under
    `repos/rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer`. It parses `-X POST`,
    `--method=POST` and `-XPOST`, and treats `-f`/`-F`/`--input` as a write
    unless the method is explicitly `GET`.
  - Repo names compare case-insensitively, with `github.com/`, `https://`
    and `.git` forms accepted. `gh repo ...` also accepts the fork as a
    positional argument.
  - Commands are tokenised with `shlex`. Unquoted newlines and backticks
    separate commands. Leading `NAME=value`, `env`, `command`, `sudo`,
    `xargs` and absolute paths are seen through, and `bash -c`, `sh -c` and
    `eval` strings are checked recursively.
  - A command it cannot parse is blocked if it looks like a `gh` write and
    does not name the fork.
- `.claude/settings.json`: registers the hook. The diff is the one added
  entry.
- `AGENTS.md`: replaces the long `--repo` bullet with a two-line rule that
  keeps the reason and says a hook enforces it, so agents other than Claude
  Code still see it. The repo-conventions bullet now says `.claude/hooks/`
  and its `Bash` entry are this repo's own and Entire leaves them alone.
- `tests/test_gh_repo_hook.py`: 59 cases, 33 blocked and 26 allowed.

## Verification

- `uv run pytest`: 534 passed. `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean.
- Rod confirmed in a fresh session that the hook registers (`/hooks`) and
  that Entire leaves the entry alone.
- Eight realistic commands from the session were checked for false

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

content.text:
All 4 new findings are resolved and none are open. The changes are uncommitted and unpushed on `chore/gh-repo-hook`. The full suite passes (554 tests), and ruff and format are clean.

The trail's default listing hides findings on code that has since changed. Earlier it showed the first nine as stale while they were all resolved. If the counts look odd in the UI, `--freshness any` shows them.

**Resolved**
- **High, `$(...)` inside double quotes:** the hook now pulls out `$(...)` bodies, and backtick bodies inside double quotes, and checks them recursively. `echo "$(gh pr create)"` and `url="$(gh pr create)"` are now blocked. A heredoc body is now treated as data and stripped first, so a PR body that mentions `gh pr view` doesn't trip it.
- **Medium, wrappers and shell keywords:** I added per-wrapper tables for flags that take a value (`env -u`, `nice -n`, `sudo -u`, `xargs -I` and others). `timeout`, `setsid` and `stdbuf` are now wrappers. `if`/`then`/`do`/`{`/`!` are skipped, and `<(` and `>(` are command separators. I took the finding's narrower option, not the "second pass" one.
- **Low, bypasses text parsing can't close:** the hook docstring now states them: calls built at run time, nesting beyond three levels, and an unparseable command that names the fork. I did **not** add the suggested `GH_REPO` env var to `settings.json`, because the finding itself says it is unverified for `gh api`. It is your call if you want it.
- **Low, `gh repo` positional:** only the first positional after the verb now counts, so `gh repo sync <upstream> --source <fork>` is blocked.

**Check:** I added 20 test cases, so the hook has 79 and the suite is at 554. All were red before the fix, apart from two guard cases that passed from the start, as intended. I also ran eleven realistic commands from this session and none were wrongly blocked.

**Worth knowing:** the old hook blocked my own Bash command mid-task, a Python heredoc whose text contained `gh pr create` and an apostrophe. That is the false positive I'd listed as a known gap. The heredoc stripping fixes it, and I confirmed that case is now allowed.

PR #8's description still lists the two gaps (`$(...)` in double quotes, and `sudo -u`) and the unquoted-heredoc false positive as open. All three are now fixed, and it says 59 test cases, not 79. Want me to commit and push this and update the description to match?

    `gh secret set` and similar are blocked.
  - Groups that cannot take `--repo` (`auth`, `config`, `gist`, `ssh-key`,

    and `.git` forms accepted. `gh repo ...` also accepts the fork as a
    positional argument.
  - Commands are tokenised with `shlex`. Unquoted newlines and backticks
    separate commands. Leading `NAME=value`, `env`, `command`, `sudo`,
    `xargs` and absolute paths are seen through, and `bash -c`, `sh -c` and

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash

```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the

  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash

entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

HOOK = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / ".claude/hooks/require-gh-repo.py"
FORK = "rodbegbie/claude-md-optimizer"
UPSTREAM = "geuneda/claude-md-optimizer"


def run_hook(command: str) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
    payload = json.dumps({"tool_input": {"command": command}})
    return subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, str(HOOK)],
        input=payload,
        text=True,
        capture_output=True,
        check=False,
    )

        "cd x && gh pr ready 7",
        f"gh api repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues -f title=x",
        f"gh api -X POST repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues",
        "gh release create v1",
        "echo $(gh pr create --title x)",
        "GH_TOKEN=x gh pr create --title t",
        "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh pr create --title t",
        "command gh pr create --title t",
        "env GH_TOKEN=x gh pr create --title t",

        "x=`gh pr create --title t`",
        'bash -c "gh pr create --title t"',

        "echo pr | xargs gh",
        f"gh api --method=POST repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues",

        f"gh api repos/{FORK}-evil/issues -f title=x",
        f"gh api repos/{UPSTREAM}/issues -f body=repos/{FORK}",
        "gh api graphql -f query=x",
        "gh repo fork",
        "gh repo sync",
        f"gh workflow run ci.yml --repo {UPSTREAM}",
        "gh secret set TOKEN",
        "gh run rerun 123",
        "gh variable set X",
        "gh cache delete --all",
        "gh pr create --title \"it's (unterminated quote",
        'gh issue comment 1 --body "oops',
        'echo "$(gh pr create --title t)"',
        'url="$(gh pr create --title t)"',
        'echo "`gh pr create --title t`"',
        "env -u GH_TOKEN gh pr create --title t",
        "xargs -I {} gh pr create --title t",
        "nice -n 10 gh pr create --title t",
        "sudo -u root gh pr create --title t",
        "timeout 30 gh pr create --title t",
        "if true; then gh pr create --title t; fi",

content.text:
All 3 open findings on trail 5 are resolved and none are open. The changes are uncommitted and unpushed on `chore/gh-repo-hook`. The full suite passes (565 tests), ruff and format are clean, and none of my 11 realistic commands were wrongly blocked.

**Resolved**
- **High, `gh repo sync` with flag values:** `gh repo sync --source <fork> <upstream>` used to pass, because the source was mistaken for the destination. The hook now collects every `owner/repo`-style argument after the verb, flag values included, and requires all of them to be the fork.
- **High, PR URL beats `--repo`:** `gh pr comment <upstream PR URL> --repo <fork>` passed, but `gh` resolves the URL first and so comments on upstream. A PR or issue URL argument must now point at the fork even when `--repo` names it. The check only fires when the whole argument is a URL, so a PR body that mentions an upstream link is unaffected.
- **Medium, heredoc substitutions:** `cat <<EOF` followed by `$(gh pr create ...)` executes, but I was stripping every heredoc body. Unquoted heredocs now keep their `$(...)` and backtick bodies for checking. Quoted heredocs stay literal data, which keeps PR and commit bodies safe.

**Check:** I added 11 test cases, 5 block and 6 allow. The 5 block cases failed before the fix and the 6 allow cases were guards. The hook now has 90 cases and the suite is at 565.

**Side effect:** the new `gh repo` rule is deliberately conservative. A branch name like `feature/x`, passed as a flag value to a `gh repo` command, looks like a repo and blocks the command. That is rare, and the fix is to name the fork.

Shall I commit and push this to PR #8? The description will then need new numbers (90 test cases, 565 tests, 16 findings) and the two new behaviours.
